utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances today, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, I'm Tom Hannis, with our intern Rose Cameron, and my Case Manager Sebastiaan van Hooydonk.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Eugene O'Sullivan, appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Aleksandar Aleksic, Miroslav Cuskic, Gillian Kelly, and Milena Dzudovic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Aleksandar Lazarevic appearing for Mr. Tomislav Kovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I had asked for five minutes just to make two requests: One was to request -- I wanted to tender an exhibit that was shown to the witness, but late in the day I was tired, my learned friends intervened, and I forgot. Beginning at transcript pages 27184 through 27186, I was showing the witness 65 ter 30046. And it's tab number 135 in the Prosecution's list. It's a 30 July 1992 appointment of Mr. Drljaca as SJB chief by Mr. Zupljanin. I note that it's on Mr. Zecevic's list this morning as something to talk to the witness about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I do object, Your Honours. I anticipated -- that is why I put it on the list. I anticipated that Mr. Hannis will seek to tender it this morning. But if you -- if I correctly remember, the witness confirmed that this document was illegal and that he didn't know anything about it, but presumed it to be illegal. Therefore, I see no basis -- apart from all other objections that I already stated yesterday about the late disclosure and the inappropriateness of the time that the Office of the Prosecutor is seeking to tendered these documents, I object on this specific document because there is no -- there has been -- there has been no connection established with the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, you were about to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I join the submission, what Mr. Zecevic say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may reply. The witness didn't challenge the authenticity. He took issue with -- he said it was illegal because centre chiefs didn't have the authority to appoint. But I pointed out to him that he apparently wasn't aware of the 25 April decision 01-25/92, which is referenced in the document, which is in the evidence in our case as 1D73, which shows that Mr. Stanisic at that time delegated authority to centre chiefs to appoint SJB chiefs. It indicated they need to get -- they needed to consult, I think, or get permission from the minister, but the document itself that's being tendered indicates that there was prior approval by the minister. So we think we've established sufficient authenticity. We think is relevant and probative on the issues, and we think it should be admitted. Defence argument should go to the weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Dealing -- Yes, Mr. Krgovic. You have something to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may add one thing. The timing for the OTP tendering this document. This document is not part of the personal file of Mr. Drljaca. The OTP had this document much earlier and they had an opportunity to discuss with the witnesses who were aware of the way of the appointment of Mr. Drljaca, and there were witnesses who spoke about retroactivity and how these decisions were adopted and antedated. However, this witness, does not constitute a nexus between him and this document and cannot offer a foundation for its admission. The OTP could have done that much earlier by pointing out to the -- the connection and explaining how this came about. We had, for example, with witnesses Miskovic and Jankovic, and there was ample opportunity for the OTP to come up with this document and put it to competent witnesses who could be able to explain why this document was issued as it was. This is prejudicial to us at this stage, and we don't have a chance to provide proper explanation about the origin of this document because we don't have available appropriate witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may add, Your Honours. I'm sorry to take up the time. The submission which Mr. Hannis made concerning 1D73 is not price and it is not correct. First of all, the document does not say what Mr. Hannis is -- is suggesting, but something completely different. The key point here is, Your Honours, that we have been disclosed the personal file of -- of one Simo Drljaca. This personal file does not contain this document, nor the approval of the -- of the -- of the minister for the appointment of -- of -- of Simo Drljaca. Furthermore, in the proceedings before this Tribunal, in Stakic, the Defence of Dr. Stakic approached the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska requesting the appointment of Simo Drljaca in 1992. And -- and the information that they received is contained in this file, the personal file of Simo Drljaca, stating that they do not have the letter of appointment of Simo Drljaca from 1992 but only the -- the documents starting from 1994 onwards. Therefore, I see there -- I don't see any basis for -- for the submission of -- or -- to -- to -- to tender this document made by the Prosecution. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, could I hear you only on this matter of disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, my information is this document was disclosed to the Defence on the 21st of July, 2010. And I don't have presently the information from our MIF sheet indicating when and how we received it. But I can check on that if that's pertinent or necessary for your final decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it is necessary to repeat what would have been said yesterday in terms of material which the Prosecution may have had in its possession and chose not to advance when it was -- or to tender when its case was being presented. And in terms of the objection to the instant document as being in the words of the witness illegal, of course, the document speaks -- what the document says is what it says. The witness's view on the regularity - my word, not his - is a matter of evidence which should have to be taken into account when the time for assessment is made. So the document is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2463, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My second request was to re-open my cross to show the witness one document which is tab number 75 in the Prosecution's list. It's 65 ter number 30032. It's dated the 5th of November, 1992, from the command of the Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade. It relates to the November 5th collegium meeting, which Mr. Stanisic was chairing but left before the third agenda item along with Mr. Kusmuk, Mr. Karisik, and Mr. Radovic because of a problem in Zvornik. It's a combat report and it talks about the problem that broke out between the special police and the military police and has an urgent request that the ministers for national defence and interior come to Zvornik. I did get in yesterday another document that indicated that the minister and General Gvero had shown up in Zvornik to deal with the problem, but this was sort of an intervening document to complete the connection between the event and the appearance of the minister. It relates to issues regarding communication and co-ordination between the military and the police, and that's why I seek to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You -- you phrased your request as being -- to be permitted to show the witness a document. I expect that there will be a consequential application and no doubt we will hear from the other side, if and when that consequential application is made. So the witness may be -- if the usher would please escort the witness to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Perhaps in the meantime, we could, Mr. Hannis, with the tendering of the Koroman and Drljaca documents. You sorted that out with the Registry, but we have to have it on record.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have sent an e-mail to them and to the Defence listing, I think, for Koroman there were three individual documents and for Drljaca there were four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Well, as I understand it, we should now admit -- you clean up the -- the 65 ter numbers. The documents. And we should now admit 65 ter 3042 and 65 ter 30043; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That would be my request. We have removed the pages that we didn't talk about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So we can -- we can do that, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. If -- unless there's a specific --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- Defence objection to any.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sorry. Yes, we do object, and for the same reason I stated before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes. But we -- unless I'm wrong, we decided upon the objection, but my question whether you object now is whether there is something about the clean-up and the -- the way the documents are presented now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure, Your Honours, on which documents we are talking about. I have -- I'm trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We're talking about the documents from the personal files of Malko Koroman and Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But I don't -- I have a number of different documents with the same 65 ter number, and I'm not sure which ones are -- are the ones that Mr. Hannis is seeking to tender. That is -- that is my problem at the moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I certainly have no problem, if he needs to take more time, Your Honour. We did identify by specific ERN page numbers the B/C/S page numbers that we're seeking to tender under those two 65 ter exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: To assist you, Mr. Zecevic, if I may build on what Judge Delvoie has said, we have already ruled on the admissibility. It's merely a question of you're being satisfied as to the tidying up exercise, so we would hear from you later on that while you familiarise yourself with the product that has now been --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, and I appreciate, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, to you sir. Again, at the start of another day's hearing, I remind you of your solemn declaration. Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, I apologise, I thought we were finished but I have one more document to show you and ask you about this morning. The usher will show you a hard copy in a moment. It's dated the 5th of November and this relates to what we discussed yesterday about the 5th --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we have the tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. This is tab number 75. 65 ter 30032.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You remember yesterday we were talking about the collegium meeting on the 5th of November during which Mr. Stanisic, Mr. Kusmuk and, I think, Mr. Radovic left early to go to Zvornik, and we saw one document that reflected that the minister and General Gvero had actually gone. I wanted to show you this one and ask you to look at item number 4. This is from the Zvornik Light Brigade. And item 4 says: "Last night around 2200, a serious conflict broke out between members of the brigade's military police and the RS special unit stationed in Zvornik. The situation extremely urgent [sic] but remains under the brigade commander's control. It's urgently requested that the ministers for national Defence and of the interior come to Zvornik." Did you know -- this is dated the 5th of November and Mr. Stanisic and the others actually left a collegium meeting on the 5th of November to go. Do you know that that was in connection with this event about the conflict between the military police and the RS special unit in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose there was no special conflict. I think it was a purely military conflict among individuals, so I don't know what you think is important in this entire context. So this is a conflict between soldiers, where people gathered in a single area and it had to do with military conduct. I don't know what you would like to elicit from me with regard to this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, the fact that the minister and -- and three high-level MUP officials left a collegium meeting, and those things only happen about once a month, seems to suggest that this was important. Surely Mr. Stanisic couldn't have gone off to every conflict between police and -- and -- and the military; right? He wouldn't have had time to do anything else. Why was this one so urgent; if you know?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it should have been urgent. The outcome of a serious conflict are always dead or wounded people. In this particular instance, this did not happen. This was a simple matter of relations between young servicemen. There was a special unit deployed in that town after paramilitary units had been removed from there. After they had eliminated Zuc and other paramilitary formations, they arrived there. But I'm sure you had an opportunity to explore that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. I have no further questions, Your Honour. I would tender it just to show the connection between the meeting and the later arrival of the minister and make whatever arguments I can from that at some later day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is there a connection -- is there, from what you have thus far elicited, established a connection, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think this the link between the meeting which shows that the minister and the other three individuals left and the other document that we got in yesterday showing that the minister and General Gvero had arrived. This is the request that initiated the departure from the meeting which resulted in the showing up later the same day. It's inextricably intertwined with the other two documents in evidence, I believe, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I don't know why the caution post hoc ergo propter hoc comes to mind, but I may be wrong. Mr. Zecevic, you have an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is not disputed that the minister left, for an urgent business, the collegium on the 5th of November. So I don't -- I don't really -- I don't really see the purpose because this has nothing to do with the charges. It is completely irrelevant event for the purposes of this trial, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, you wanted to add something? I saw you moving. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic submits everything that I wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's been an important issue in this trial. The relations between the military and the police, resubordination, who controls who, whether it is co-ordinated action, et cetera. The fact that the military makes an urgent request for the minister to show up and both ministers show up within hours is something that may be of importance in your final resolution of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, when it said the conflict between members of the military police and the Republika Srpska special unit stationed in Zvornik, am I right to understand that to be the special police unit?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I -- I believe so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I see Mr. Zecevic nodding.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2464, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. I have apparently misled you in one aspect of this. My Case Manager pointed out to me that 65 ter 30033, which is the other document dated the 5th of November about the minister and General Gvero showing up, which I discussed with the witness yesterday, wasn't tendered and is not in. But I would -- I would tender it now, and I apologise for having believed and led to you believe that it was already in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So that, too, is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kovac.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2465, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kovac.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, I would have to ask you a big favour. Since we both speak the same language, we are going to overlap unless we make a pause between each question and answer that you give me, and this is going to be -- to make life very difficult to the interpreters who are doing a fantastic job and who interpreted everything that you discussed with Mr. Hannis and the Judges over the past two or three days. Now please pay attention to that. Now, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have assistance from the usher, in that he be given a binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The first document that I wish to show you is marked tab 149. That's P2459. You can find numbers on the side and please look for 149, and you'll have no problem in locating it. Sir, the document shown to you by the Prosecutor yesterday is this one. You remember that. It's an information that came from Ilidza on 13 June. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis read a quote to you, but I think that inadvertently he omitted read paragraph 2 on the last page, and I'm going to read it out to you. It reads -- and it's page 3 in the e-court in the Serbian and I suppose number 2 in the English. It reads: "The National Security Service department in Ilidza Serbian public security station as well as the services of this SJB are working on shedding more light to and on documenting Milic's above-mentioned acts." Are you aware of the fact that they investigated Milic's activities?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am. But, as I insisted yesterday, I would really like to have the previous paragraph read as well. I can do it, or maybe you can do it, because that will give us a full picture. There were groups who came from outside of Ilidza and they tried to persuade them to attack the station, the public security station, and also to organise the assassination of the station's commander. This was going to give us a full picture of the situation. And now I can answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm merely interested in one thing, sir, and since our time is limited please focus on my questions. Here's what I'm only interested in: Do you know and is it true what we read here that the National Security Service and the public security station investigated all illegal activities of this person and his group, including, of course, the attack on the public security station. Are you aware of that or not?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, I am. And certainly we launched a series of activities to follow and shed more light on the group headed by this Milic. It was a serious case for us, and it was a delicate matter because he had links to former National Security Service staff. And before the war, the Croatian Intelligence Service gave him the task to -- to disrupt the interethnic relations at Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, this person eventually got killed or died due to an overdose.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This person was found dead in specific circumstances. He had overdosed and we knew that, apart from these other activities, he was also a link in the transit chain, transport chain of drugs travelling to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You also discussed another document with Mr. Hannis yesterday and I'm speaking about tab 150; document P648. You remember that you also discussed this document with Mr. Hannis yesterday and you did it at length.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At the last page of this document, we see the signature of the person who drafted it. It says Ilidza public security station chief, Tihomir Glavas. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you commented on this and said about this document that this is an epic inclination which is understandable, bearing in mind the war-time context and that they overly praised you to indirectly praise themselves and be decorated. And you also said that to your mind, Tihomir Glavas was a solid police officer. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let's go to page -- pages 6 and 7 of this document where the proposals for decorations can be found. Your name is the first one mentioned, and let's go to item 5.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 5 is Tihomir Glavas, chief of Hadzic SJB, assistant to chief for the police of SJB Ilidza, and then chief of station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, is this the same Tihomir Glavas who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the same man.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In other words, he proposes himself for a medal in a document that he signed.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So much about the value of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. That's a submission for final arguments, not an appropriate comment when the witness is testifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I withdraw that. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, sir, when you came to the Ministry of the Interior - I mean, the ministry headquarters - if I understood your evidence well, you said that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please give the witness some more water. He's asking for water. Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, if I understood your evidence correctly, meaning that the consolidation process of the MUP at that moment had already begun.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You also said in your evidence that Mico Stanisic spoke to you before you were transferred to the MUP, and I believe that you said that there were stories about him telling you that he needed professionals in the police with experience and moral integrity to create the RS MUP properly, and that everything be done in accordance with the law. Have I summed up your evidence correctly?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In a nutshell, he needed people who were police officers through and through and not loyal to local communities or open to other influences. And, of course, he needed people with enough energy to implement the things that were necessary. The Ministry of Interior had to be completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I remember well, you mentioned in that context that one of his demands was that those people be without party ties. In other words, independent from party politics and, in fact, true professionals.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was along those lines. I believe that when he chose me for that post, he, at the same time, outlined the course of action of the Public Security Service and made a statement regarding relations with politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the course of that consolidation process, some activities were initiated, so please confirm whether I'm right. After the opening of the corridor, conditions were created for integrating the RS MUP into a whole and establishing links along lines of work.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The action to significantly reduce the reserve force was begun.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: An action was initiated with regard to individuals who were admitted to the police without previous vetting to be discharged from the police and put at the disposal of the army.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Public security stations began to be set up, and at MUP headquarters, there was a separation of the police administration and the crime enforcement administration.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The consolidation and setting up of the National Security Service.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The initiation of the consolidation and setting up of some CSBs, such as Bijeljina, Sarajevo, Trebinje, and the re-establishment of the Doboj centre.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The abolishment of various so-called special police units that had been set up by some public security stations, CSBs, Crisis Staffs, and the like, and the setting up of a special unit detachment with each CSB under the command of the special police brigade, headed by Karisik and the ministry.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Based on this new, stronger position of the special police brigade commanded by Karisik and the ministry, as of June 1992, this brigade took on paramilitaries in Brcko, Bijeljina, Zvornik and so on?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Wasn't the intention of the RS MUP at that moment to settle accounts with all kinds of crime and put an end to war crimes, including illegal camps and the like?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In order to achieve all these objectives that I mentioned - but I add that this is not a comprehensive list - some personnel changes were made, both in the ministry headquarters as well as in the public security stations on the ground?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's a fact that you also came to the RS MUP in that framework of personnel changes.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me when I say that this was a process that was started and on which you also embarked from the outset?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What was the desire behind that process? The setting up of the rule of law and make sure that the ministry functioned in accordance with the law?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may give a more comprehensive answer. I have been brief so far. One of the motives of us professional police officers in Bosnia-Herzegovina, when we decided the police of -- to leave the police of Bosnia-Herzegovina, apart from the need to side with the -- our own people, it was much more important, actually, when we came to the sad insight that we were working in a criminal MUP headed by Alija Delimustafic and in a state organisation where the institutions are in the service of one people and one party, and at that time, it was the Muslim people and the SDA party. As a professional at Ilidza, I was being humiliated. The president of the then-Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic, when he came to an official state conference, he was -- or security was provided to him by an illegal organisation called the Patriotic League and the MUP couldn't get near him. All that induced us to create a MUP that was up to the criteria we were imbued with during our training and not a MUP like that of Bosnia-Herzegovina. A MUP that would not be ruled by individuals, parties, or para-parties, even if they are from the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, one of the ways to reach those goals that you mentioned was the need for the MUP to keep law and order, to prosecute offenders, to submit criminal offences to the relevant institutions, and do everything that a MUP has to do in a country, in accordance with the law and the constitution?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, since for a while in 1992 you were a very close associate of Mr. Mico Stanisic, do you have reason to doubt that these were also the goals of Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In 1992 we were totally on the same wavelength with regard to these things. At that time, I had the greatest powers to -- to put my ideals and -- or, rather, ideas about the structure and functioning of the MUP into practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in the documents we received, I found some statements of yours; for example, that, in your opinion, Mico Stanisic, in 1992, burned out in his efforts to set up a MUP in accordance with the law and the way it should be and cracked down on all types of crime, and that he was removed from his post because he lost political support for his efforts. Do you stand by that statement?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, was the loss of that political support in late 1992 a result, in your view, of precisely these efforts on your part within the MUP to crack down on all types of crime and prosecute the perpetrators thereof?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in your evidence yesterday, you told us that everything that was, in your view, done positively by you in 1992, with a view to improving the conditions in the MUP of role, was practically reversed in 1993 while Mr. Ratko Adzic headed the MUP?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: If I may go back to the previous topic; that is, Mr. Stanisic's burnout in 1992. You say that you have -- you found "some statements of yours; for example ..." Could you tell us what documents you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I have -- I believe it's -- it's -- I have found it on -- on -- on two -- two places, but, at this point I can only give a reference to one. It's the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's P841. And I can quote directly from -- from this. This is an interview of Mr. Tomo Kovac from 1996, 1st of March, 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: For me, it's okay. For the moment we have the exact reference. It's okay for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: To be on the safe side, I will remind you of your exact words. "Mico Stanisic burnt out while performing his role twice. He approached his tasks with great enthusiasm and burnt out." Do you recall these words?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, we spoke of the situation in 1993. It is a fact, is it not, that after Mico Stanisic's deposition as well as yours and other MUP staff, at a point in time when Ratko Adzic was appointed minister of the interior of Republika Srpska, not only were all the activities for the betterment of the organisation that were undertaken in 1992 neutralised, but the situation went back to the starting point or even to a state of affairs that was worse than it had been at the start of the process.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please help yourself. I apologise for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. This process was halted and matters took a different course. We got an individual who had come from the Crisis Staff who had a different mindset which had an idea of how things were to function locally but had no idea of how the rule of law should be enforced and how the institutions at the central level were to function. We mounted some sort of resistance to what he was introducing at that level in the MUP, but the process was, nevertheless, halted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "the process was, nevertheless, halted," you mean the process of betterment which was launched in 1992.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I meant the process to complete the building of the institutions and staff with a view to enforcing a rule of law, which is one of the basic tenets of any functioning state.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you will agree with me, will you not - you did say that a moment ago - that what was peculiar about the situation, which characterised the year 1992, was the existence of these Crisis Staffs and the power, the enormous power they wielded locally where they were absolute masters of the situation?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the point of the breakup of the state, they were definitely in that position. All the decisions were made at one level only. There were no two-tier decision-making structures. They had everything under them: The army, the organisation, the municipality. And even the better part of the police, although we were the first ones to leave that circle because we had already shaped up our structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you say that already you had the contours of the ministry in place. The power that the -- that the Crisis Staffs had adversely affected the MUP, its authority and effective control that it had over its elements.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is impossible to generalise across the board. There were places where the leadership of the Crisis Staff was normal, as it were, whereas there were also places where we had our public security stations headed by individuals who were strong enough to prevail and make sure that things were done in accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, what I said about this adverse effect on the work the MUP, it was felt but not everywhere. It was, though, a negative manifestation of the time, was it not?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I -- up to some 30 per cent, which was already enough, to create enormous problems for us. And, as a result, this is where we are today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the power that the Crisis Staffs wielded locally was reflected in the authorities in general and especially in the central authorities?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course. Because all these local authorities had their representatives in the assembly. And the National Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time was the highest political and legislative body which had an influence, in part, over the executive as well. And as a result of that, they were able to topple three governments in war time, which is not an occurrence you would easily see around the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you spoke of certain changes in the staff with Mr. Hannis and Their Honours. You spoke of certain staff having been removed. I have a couple of cases in my hands here, and I'd like to you comment on them. You will remember that yesterday you commented on a case related to Mr. Stevan Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think you explained this yesterday. We have the entire documentation on file. But I would like you to clarify the transcript. Page 27071, and I'll read out the relevant part in English so that you would get the accurate quote. [In English] "That was obvious while Mr. Adzic was minister and wanted to do some things that were contrary to the wishes of us professionals. I understood it to be Mr. Stanisic's wish to do the things that I was doing. And it follows from some documents that Minister Stanisic was involved in some proceedings, except in the case of Todorovic." [Interpretation] Well, this is why I am about to ask you to clarify this. But let me summarise this. The fact of the matter is, Mr. Kovac, that at the time when Mico Stanisic was minister in 1992, you, as chief of administration, deployed inspectors of the administration of the MUP to Samac to a fact -- to carry out a fact-finding mission; did you not?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The chief of the Security Services Centre, Mr. Bjelosevic, proposed in 1992 that a new individual be pointed as chief of the public security in Samac - that's to say, Petar Cancar - because, as he put it, of frequent and gross misconduct in the service on the part of Stevan Todorovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The fact that Stevan Todorovic, at some point in 1992, was taken into custody. That was another fact that was listed; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in relation to Malko Koroman, are you aware that Malko Koroman was the chief of the public security station at Pale, pursuant to a decision issued by the minister, Alija Delimustafic, in 1991?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you were shown a document yesterday, 65 ter 10 -- or, rather, yes, 10373, which is tab 151. It's a document dated the 11th of January, 1993. And Acting Minister Radomir Njegus signed the document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Acting assistant minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this is a cover letter relating to Malko Koroman; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, at this point in time, on the 11th of January, 1993, Mico Stanisic was already removed from his position in the ministry, and you, too, if I understand your evidence, correctly, had been divested of all powers by your leadership as of the 1st of January?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was supposed to be deputy minister, but I actually stayed behind as chief of the police administration. So this is a document sent by the assistant minister to the chief of the administration.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat what he said last. It was too soft.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The witness is asked by the interpreters to repeat his last answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm Sorry, Your Honours. Sorry to interrupt, Your Honours. Did you want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Did you hear -- did you hear what I --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So if the witness can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, please speak slowly and clearly and say briefly what it was that you said.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It transpires from this document that it was sent to the chief of the police administration which was the position I was discharging at the time, and it was sent by the acting assistant minister. So the new minister had already appointed assistant -- acting assistant minister. You could already tell that I was the third in the hierarchy of the ministry at the time, and this was definitely during the time of Minister Ratko Adzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry to intervene. But could I ask my learned friend to clarify, because it sounds like the witness is suggesting that Mr. Njegus is the acting minister for the MUP rather than the acting minister for -- assistant minister for administration for legal and administrative affairs. I just want to be sure that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain this?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't mean the minister. But you can see the new hierarchy that is in place --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, sorry. A moment. You have probably misunderstood. This is the question. Look at the document. On the 11th of January, 1993, did Radomir Njegus write this letter as the acting assistant minister or in some other capacity?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can clearly says that he was writing this as the acting assistant minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. It's my understanding there are many -- there were many assistant ministers in the MUP for the various administrations, police administrations, communications, et cetera, as opposed to acting minister, and that's -- that's where my confusion lies. Is it acting minister as Mr. Kovac was at times where he acted for Mr. Stanisic in 1992, or is it acting minister for one of the ten administrations within the MUP headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you clarify this issue for Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me recall that at the time there were only two assistant ministers within the organisation during Stanisic; that was Dragan Kijac and Tomislav Kovac. Under the new organisation -- or, rather, under the new minister, Radomir Njegus was chief of the administration for personnel. But since it says here that he is acting assistant minister, this means that he was appointed by the minister and not by the government. That was the power of the then-minister who could appoint a person to be acting assistant minister. So he was assistant minister - that's to say, Radomir Njegus - under the authority of the minister and not of the government. Because under the law it was the government that was supposed to appoint assistant ministers, but he was here as acting assistant minister until such point as the government may decide to appoint him to the post of assistant minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think you have clarified this issue sufficiently. Sir, when you say that during the time Mico Stanisic was minister there were two assistant ministers, and you named Dragan Kijac and yourself, you meant the chiefs of the National Security Service, Dragan Kijac, and the public security administration of which you were the chief at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, as far as I know, there were two assistant ministers at the time and no more. And I explained as far as I could tell what the difference was between an acting assistant minister and an assistant minister. Now, I don't know if there was somebody there from before and may have been removed. This is something I can't go into.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to show you another document, which I believe was shown to you yesterday, although I'm not sure. Now let us go back to Malko Koroman. You know that he was appointed by Mr. Alija Delimustafic as the chief of the Pale SJB back in 1991?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let's look at document 65 ter 30042. That's tab 152. And it's a decision on temporary assignment of Malko Koroman dated 1st April 1992. Have you managed to find the document? Tab 152. No, that's not the document. It's ERN 03240401.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah. I think the problem, Your Honour, I think this is one of the documents from which we had removed the ones that I didn't show the witness, and we only have in e-court now the ones that I showed the witness about Mr. Koroman yesterday. And I didn't show him the April 1992 appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, Your Honours. I wasn't aware that these documents had been withdrawn from the e-court. Now the only way would be that we probably put it on the ELMO. I don't see what else can we do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, could we take the break --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yeah, yeah -- no, no. This is -- this is the -- yes. This is the document. No, no, we found it. Thank you very much. I'm sorry, I wasn't aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, look at the document on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it, and I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Sir, you see that pursuant to this decision Malko Koroman is temporarily assigned to Ministry of Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as an inspector at the Sarajevo CSB, so he was not appointed chief of the SJB Pale?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It's clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew what his status was when I joined the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I don't know whether this document is in evidence now or whether you want to tender it. Is it in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, honestly, I'm not sure, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I don't think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it is as another exhibit. It's P1416.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Should we say that parties check this during the break. Would that be a good idea?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I wanted to suggest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Registrar has confirmed that it is in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Much obliged. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can the Registrar tell us what the exhibit number which.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1416, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I see the time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we continue in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovac, a minute ago, I showed you this decision relating to Malko Koroman. Did you know that back in April 1992, Malko managed to assemble 3.000 people at Pale who, with the use of weapons, prevented his dismissal from the position of the SJB chief?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had heard of that, but I wasn't participating in that. I was at Ilidza at the time. I heard of this information. So these were the remnants of small communities, and this is something that was reflected in the communities that had Crisis Staffs and their own local institutions without any consciousness or awareness that they should be subordinated to higher authorities, so people were not skillful in acting in a stately manner. So this one of the most striking example of that that we encountered.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to show you document -- tab 37. It's 1D644. While we are waiting for you to find the document, let me ask you this: You know Ostoja Minic?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: He was an inspector in the administration for crime control at the MUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is a report on the inspection and the activities of the Pale SJB which relates to the period April through to December 1993 [as interpreted]. It was compiled on the 8th of March, 1993. Let us look at the last and the penultimate pages which contains proposals for future activities. That's page 5 in the Serbian, and I suppose it's the same page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Proposals -- I'm sorry. Proposals begin on page 6 of the English for e-court [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Hannis. [Interpretation] So page 6 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Have you found it? It's on page 5. There's a subtitle which says: "Proposed Tasks and Measures." And it's at the bottom of page five.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I have page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Look at the --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And within the context of the proposed tasks and measures, it is said that additional statements should be taken from the following employees, and then we see the names of Malko Koroman and other senior officials from the public station. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now move to page 6 in the Serbian; page 7 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You're going to see it shortly on your screen. And look at item 2. One of the proposed measures by Ostoja Minic was that once the statements are taken from the proposed Pale SJB employees, it is necessary to analyse it for possible elements of crime, the crime administration in the Sarajevo CSB, senior officers should be informed accordingly. And once the criminal responsibility has been assessed, criminal reports should be submitted to the competent prosecutor's office. Do you see this?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was this proposal made by Inspector Ostoja Minic in accordance with the Law on Interior?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. But it also has to be in line with the Law on Criminal Procedure, because that also governs such matters -- measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, since, in the MUP of Republika Srpska, you discharged the most serious duties, such as acting minister and minister and assistant minister, I suppose that you are quite familiar with the political aspect of running a ministry.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When I say this, I'm referring to the situation in which you, as a minister, with a view to improving the operation and performance of the ministry, are in a position in which sometimes you must make certain political and strategic compromises?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please answer that question?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: These compromises were made in order for the ministry to achieve certain results while you were in office.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at least while I was there, these compromises had more to do with personnel solutions, not so much in the domain of the law. So these were feasible compromises because we were really exposed to strong pressures concerning personnel issues. However, when it came to the implementation of the law, these kind of pressures were rather more subtle and not so open.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I was particularly referring to personnel issues and the compromises that had to be taken and were unavoidable, which is only understandable when it comes to any ministry anywhere, including Republika Srpska. Now, let me quote an example for you and I would kindly ask you to comment on it, on the basis of your good knowledge of these issues. Mr. Kovac, if you have a situation in which certain executive from your ministry, and you are not satisfied with his performance, nevertheless, enjoys undivided support of the political structures and the population in the territory of the police station that he is at the head of, would you dismiss such person by utilizing your powers and authorities and thereby risk to be faced with a public outrage and ultimately your dismissal; or would you first remove such an executive from the territory in which he enjoys such support by offering him a pompous position without any substantial function? As you put it yesterday, would you put him on ice?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The skill of management, especially in terms of implementing the law and pursuing the decided policy, is that you try to remove the undesirables in the least painful way possible. So with a view of doing that, we did so-called rotations. We move them from the centre to the republic, or we recommended them to be appointed advisors to prime minister or somebody else. So with a new staff we managed to fulfill our tasks. And quite often we made it easier for those people who were in certain positions, because by shifting them to other positions we helped them because they didn't have capability to undertake proper legal or other measures in this environment. Sometimes the fate of their families was at stake as well, so this was another obstacle that prevented them from implementing these measures, so that is the reason why we resorted to giving them these kind of decorations and probably sent them to retirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you agreed with me that you did this in order to allow the people appointing to the posts that were vacated by other people whom you rotated to other positions, you -- in that way you would help these newcomers in establishing normal operation of a state -- of -- SJBs?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. But during my term of office, and I think that equally applies to Stanisic's time, I don't think that there were many instances of the so-called rehabilitation of such personnel. I think that this happened more frequently during the terms of office of Adzic and Rakic. This is, generally speaking, but maybe if you would analyse it in detail you would find out exactly what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, during the time that Mr. Stanisic was the minister, and also during the time when you were the minister, the rehabilitation of the personnel who had been shifted due to the reasons that we explained earlier, happened less frequently than during the terms of office of Ministers Adzic and Rakic?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It clearly stems from the decision issued at the time, and I wouldn't like to personalise this issue. You just have to look at the decisions issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in this situation, when we were discussing the personnel and staff members that had to be relocated from their home turf where they enjoyed strong support, if there were indications that such members of the staff had committed criminal offences, in your opinion, would such criminal offences be treated particularly cautiously in order to find out all the facts and then proceeding to filing a report to the prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We worked on collecting information about everyone for whom there were indications, and I don't think that there was any operative or an executive who can say that he had been prevented or stopped from collecting information or from offering his opinion. Let me quote the example of Milic [as interpreted] in the case of Pale and Samac because he was involved in that. As I said, nobody within the ministry prevented them from undertaking measures or from filing criminal reports. This equally applies to operatives or inspectors or chiefs of administrations. Only when we reach the level assembly deputies, according to the law, we had to request that they be stripped of their immunity, and there were cases like that. And Minister Stanisic was involved in these procedures. I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On page 37, line 2 of the transcript you're recorded of having mentioned the example of a certain Milic but it should be Minic; right? We remember him from Samac.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Minic is the name. I believe his first name was Ostoja. He was professional and uncompromising, and we gave him the opportunity to work the way he preferred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. He was recorded as Milic and that was the reason for my intervention. Sir, yesterday, on page 27187 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just to have a clear record, can I ask you: When you're talking about rehabilitation, do you mean reappointment?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that in my opinion means when the witness said rehabilitations, successful -- another appointment after some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But if you want me to clarify with the witness, I'm happy to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 27187, Mr. Hannis put something to you, and I'll re-read it in English. [In English] "Well, I know earlier you told us that you talked about this rotation of staff to keep some of these guys from thwarting investigations. But sending Mr. Drljaca who was suspected in connection with misconduct, at least, connected to the Koricanske Stijene case, sending him to Banja Luka as deputy chief doesn't seem to be a very good place to put him, is it?" Your answer: "Well, you are not being precise. This is an assistant centre chief, but I think he was assistant chief without specific tasks. I don't know if he really had work at the time. That's when you give a decision to somebody without any duties, to remove him, to put him on ice. And this -- but this man had stronger political support than all the rest of us together; that must have been why." [Interpretation] Do you remember that the Prosecutor put this to you and your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm just interested in whether you remember. I will ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, by shifting a person, and let's suppose that it's about Simo Drljaca here, from a municipality where he enjoys full support and where he's very powerful, you achieve, firstly, that that person is removed from his support which weakens him; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the circumstances, yes, clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Secondly, such a shift, the shifting of that person from the municipality or the place where he has support makes it possible to conduct an investigation into that person without him interfering; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And, thirdly, and possibly most importantly, the situation in the place from which that person is being taken can then be put in order and things can become legal, and the procedure in connection with prosecuting that person becomes possible?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer because we needed a break between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were too fast. Please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. These are the initial actions to establish the responsibility of any individual, but these processes take a while, up to 20 years, as we can see here. But we shouldn't -- certainly we went about it that way, to establish anybody's responsibility in a given area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And if I understood you correctly, the documents that were obtained during the process of establishing responsibility, were obtained for the purpose of initiating criminal proceedings at some point; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our immediate goal was to find out what happened, to assert -- or establish the facts, as can be seen from the reports of the Banja Luka CSB, and the inspectors carried out an audit in Prijedor pursuant to the order of the centre chief and our instruction. Those documents would first, based on which we, from the ministry HQ, established that members of the Public Security Service had committed some illegal acts beyond their remit, beyond their authority. And these are the initial elements which we thus documented.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Thank you for this clarification. Considering the positions of Malko Koroman and Simo Drljaca in their respective municipalities and the support that they enjoyed from the local bodies, Crisis Staffs, and the citizens themselves, was this approach to tackling that problem at the time fully sensible?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Only I would like to single out Malko Koroman. He was not held responsible for war crimes at any time. He wasn't even accused by the Bosniak side. He committed some other offences, but, so far, nobody has ever accused Malko Koroman of war crimes. There were illegal actions on both sides, but Malko Koroman was never suspected of war crimes. There were irregularities in his work, a lot of irregularities. But they were not that serious. Even now, 20 years after the war, nobody has ever accused him of war crimes. No official body, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Talking about crimes possibly committed by members of the MUP, the essence there is certainly their criminal responsibility, not disciplinary accountability; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly talking about war crimes, it's clear that a war crime is a criminal offence. And if anybody learns of a war crime, he must also launch disciplinary proceedings. Disciplinary proceedings can be launched without criminal accountability, but not the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I agree. But the essence is the following: If it is established that somebody committed a crime, then disciplinary accountability is understood; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. The Law on Internal Affairs imposes a duty on senior officers to launch proceedings if they learn that somebody committed criminal offences, especially in connection with discharging their duties. So they must launch proceedings against the member of the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But the purpose is filing a criminal complaint.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that too. And in order to facilitate criminal proceedings, for the perpetrator not to be in a position where he had power and where he could disrupt the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What was a disciplinary policy in place in the ministry in 1992? Can you tell us. Will you agree with me when I say that there was a quite strict disciplinary policy in place toward members of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two ways of going about these things: One was to discharge somebody from the MUP; and the other was to replace somebody from their position, especially if it was a position of authority. The most appropriate measure for cleansing the MUP, which is the term that we used at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that was done in 1992 in all cases where it was possible; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It went through a process. I can refer to the period as of August. I know how -- how fast that went then. We were strengthening the institutions and that enabled us to take energetic and comprehensive action. But you quoted some decisions that -- which show that with a few moves we removed thousands of people from the reserve force and from the ranks of active-duty officers because these people were unfit to be police officers. From the first initial stage, when many responded to either the call-up to join the reserve force out of patriotism, in the second half of the year we decided to give these people to the army and screen out all these members that we didn't need. So we reduced our numbers and, certainly, we got rid of para-groups and para-individuals who -- who stuck with the -- with police units or police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because we had a huge problem --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead but be brief.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a great problem. At one point, there was an instruction from a member of the Presidency of the RS, Biljana Plavsic, to put all volunteers under control and all individuals. And that was done by some stations initially. But, later, we went -- we had to go to great lengths to remove these people from the reserve police force and the active-duty force, for that matter, because it transpired that many of them, due to their mindset, their past, and so on, were unfit for either the reserve force or the active-duty force, and we had great problems in the process of cleansing our ranks from these individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us finish this topic of disciplinary accountability. You certainly know that the MUP, in September, adopted a rule-book on disciplinary accountability at a time of imminent threat of war, which is 1D54, at tab 158.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. And I was involved in the drafting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that rule-book shortened the disciplinary procedure. Disciplinary commissions were abolished. CSB chiefs and administration chiefs of the MUP, as well as the commander, were empowered to impose sanctions for more serious infractions. And under Article 15, the minister, in the second instance, decided about such cases, and his decision was final. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is the adoption of such a rule-book, or does it tally with the overall intentions of the ministry in 1992 to crack down on irregularities within the ministry and punish their members for their shortcomings?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that very well. I know when we were adopting this. We needed a rule-book that was operational and, yet, in accordance with the law. It had to be suitable for use in war time because under the previous rule-book - let's call it the peacetime rule-book - there was much leeway for individuals or commissions to act destructively when it comes to the launching and the conduct of disciplinary proceedings. So it was about compatibility with the times and the circumstances on the one hand and the -- our needs on the other. I made relevant proposals to the minister. I also had experience because before the war I had been a long-standing member of the disciplinary board of the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so I did have experience with efficiency and with what we wanted to get out of the -- these new rules, the effect that we wanted to achieve, and we wanted to get rid of undesirable individuals as fast and as easily as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that over 95 per cent of disciplinary proceedings in 1992 were -- resulted in appeals and the appeals were mostly dismissed in the second instance as -- and the sanction was mostly the most severe one; namely, the discharge from service?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know about it. I was involved. The centre chiefs, in the first instance, especially in connection with removal from the service, their decisions were mostly confirmed in the second instance. That was our policy at the time, and I believe that the facts and the evidence fully corroborate these decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I have only a couple of short questions left for you. A moment ago, I read out for you -- are you feeling uncomfortable or?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, I read out for you the suggestion that was put to you by Mr. Hannis yesterday in relation to Simo Drljaca. He mentioned the crime at Koricanske Stijena. You said that after the crime took place you came to learn of it but that it was within the remit of the crime prevention administration that was led by Mr. Macar; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, that in September of 1992, in connection with the Koricanske Stijene case, the Banja Luka CSB filed a criminal complaint with the prosecutor's office having jurisdiction. Do you also know that the police recovered the survivals, they found the survivals, and that their statements were taken in accordance with the Law on Criminal Procedure and that, as a result, perpetrators were being sought. Were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was aware of the fact that there was the intention to fully prosecute the case. Now, as for the various details and how far they went along is not something that I can tell you. I note that there was a process pending.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you were shown a document yesterday, P2463, which is tab 154. I think have you it in the other binder of documents. It is a longish reference in yesterday's transcript at 27184. That's the page of the transcript. I will try to summarise your evidence there. Commenting upon this document, you said that the document was not legally valid, and you provided your comments on the analysis. You told Mr. Hannis that you were very familiar with these issues and that you knew what you were talking about. I'm interested in a different aspect of the matter. Sir, every individual working for the MUP has a personnel dossier on the records; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This sort of decision and purportedly the approval of the MUP minister, which the document refers to, necessarily has to be present in the personnel file of the individual it refers to; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that the personnel file for Simo Drljaca, which is kept in the RS MUP archives, does not contain this document or the document where, apparently, the minister gave his consent, what would your response to that be?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was precisely what I was about to comment on yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you did say -- and I don't know if there's need for you to repeat it because what you did say is in the record, so please be brief.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This method of proceeding, even had the consent of the minister been given, is not in keeping with the law. Quite another thing, which I was opposed to as one of the persons in position of authority from day one, was this sort of standard procedure in terms of personnel, because I know that behind such a decision there had to have been a political support and there had to have been some political clout behind it. Because later on when there were problems in removals and all of it, the decision was brought to him by the chief of centre, and when he was supposed to be deposed, the law was applied and the chief of centre was not required. At that point they were quite familiar with the law. They knew it was the minister of the interior who had to remove them. They were also aware of a different law, and they knew how to proceed when the political circles didn't need him anymore. So this was a vicious circle that we were unable to enter, in fact. Once you embark on an unlawful situation, and once this is coupled with political interests and the situation on the ground as it is, it is impossible to man the structure or to run a structure properly. This is why, from day one, I was -- I clashed openly with all the tendencies that thwarted the process of centralisation of the MUP. And that made it impossible to have this two-tier system of either the criminal or disciplinary responsibility. It was impossible to develop the embryo of the state based on such procedure. This is a clear example of all our problems. This is something that I wanted to add yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You've completed your answer now. I have limited time. That's why I need to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have always been forthcoming when it came to that, so you will appreciate that I needed to say this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
