utterances.text: Well, I'm grateful for that. Sir, I have to go back to that issue again. The point of the matter was that, for some of the employees, as was the case here, there was strong political pressure and huge support that they enjoyed in their respective territories; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Amid the war psychoses, especially one that prevailed in the Kozara area that had suffered greatly in World War II, a new psychoses was developed, one that the prevalent feeling was that the horrible events of World War II were going to repeat themselves in that area on both sides. Some felt it harder; others less hard than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Hannis showed you yesterday a number of documents, decisions from 1994, and in doing so suggested that regardless of your evidence and your statement that it was the intention of the ministry that all the employees who were in violation of the law, including Simo Drljaca and some others, should be removed from their positions and should have proceedings instituted against them, so he suggested that the 1994 decisions were the ones that appointed these same individuals to some other posts or duties within the MUP. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please show me these documents? I didn't have an opportunity to review them properly yesterday. Is it possible to have these documents? I don't have them with me. And I need to have them to be able to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let's take it slowly, sir. I'm doing my best.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't quite clear on that yesterday, and I'd like to have a better look.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will give you the same documents that the Prosecutor showed to you yesterday. One of them is the Koroman, Malko set of documents; and the other is the Drljaca, Simo set of documents. The only problem now is that I don't have the documents anymore.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're trying to save on paper again?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's tab 153. Some of the documents were admitted only this morning, so we don't have them in the tab. I gave the witness what our assistants prepared for us from the Defence. Sir, have you had a look?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Can I keep them while I'm commenting on them? You can go ahead and put your question to me and --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Pause there for a moment. So you have had a look at the documents. You have them before you now.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, do you allow for the possibility that the reason why such decisions were issued in 1994 and later and why some of these individuals were appointed to positions within the MUP was a decision that had been made based on the political circumstances prevailing at the time, for instance, in 1994. Do you allow for that possibility?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we go back to the date, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. I object to the form of the question as it relates to any documents that were signed by this witness, because if he's the one who signed the decision like the one that's on the screen now, you don't have to ask him if he allows for the possibility. He either knows if he signed it because of political pressure or he didn't. Now he may be ask to speculate about what Mr. Stanisic or some other minister signed, but the one signed by him, certainly he must know whether he did it on his own or based on some political pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I accept, Mr. Hannis. Thank you very much. You are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You did hear what Mr. Hannis had to say. Tell us, some of the documents that you signed, were they the result of political circumstances? Were they in any way forced out of you? And did you make them under political pressure or not?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let us first clarify one thing. Let us set out Malko Koroman first. He was an individual who was appointed pursuant to these decisions to the post of, as it reads here, chief inspector of police. I didn't appoint Malko Koroman, so this is a decision on fast-track promotion to a different rank, so this isn't a decision on his appointment. Let me clarify. These decisions appointing him as chief inspector meant that, in operative terms, he was assigned to the most difficult operative missions. He was sent out into the field and, thus, it was -- he was prevented from making any important decisions back in the headquarters. For instance, people who were not given to policing duties, were not capable of performing them, I would send them out to the war-affected areas where they would have to deal with combat. So my view of Malko Koroman's case indicates that his case is completely different from that of Simo Drljaca. The appointment of Malko Koroman is something that I accept, since I was the one manning the police administration, that -- that his appointment was the result of my policy, whereby these people who were not capable of performing public security duties were sent out to perform the duties of participation in the war, as it were. And so he was treated in the same way. He had the obligation of a conscript, as it were. Just -- he was just a member of the police. But that was what he was to be doing there. And I think we've clarified Koroman. As for Simo Drljaca, in the interviews I gave on several occasions, for reasons which were the ones because of which the Trial Chamber invited me here, I spoke on behalf of the Ministry of Interior, and I said on several occasions that whenever a decision had to be taken. What was the sort of relationship I had with Zika Rakic? Oftentimes they would ask who was the minister of the two of us. I was deputy minister at the time. They asked me how it all worked. Whenever the political circles wanted to have some of their cadres appointed somewhere, well, you see, this was the time when Zika Rakic was minister. You see that he signed this. So whenever it suited them to have me deal with the matter operatively, then they would allow me to deal well it operatively. The way the policy of staffing was enforced can be seen precisely in this appointment where Simo Drljaca is appointed as chief of the public security centre in Prijedor. This was done by Zika Rakic who, himself, had been appointed there with a political mission, a mission from his political party, and his mission was that at some point where there was disagreement between us, as a minister, by virtue of his position, he would enforce the sort of personnel policy that suited them. And this is what he did. You can see that this was shortly after the departure of Stanisic, after he was removed. So it was Zivko Rakic who appointed him. An indisputable fact is that these people were appointed, but it also says something about the rotation of the various ministers and the general policy applied to the Ministry of Interior. As you look at this specific decision you see that behind the decision is Zika Rakic and behind Zika Rakic there is politics. Politics equals Zika Rakic. And then on the other side you have the professional running of the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I take it you have a clear understanding with Mr. Krgovic about the division of time allotted for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes, Your Honours. I have just two more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, was -- the second dismissal of Mico Stanisic in 1994 came as a result, again, of the political pressure for him to be removed and for this person, Rakic, to be installed in his place, and you said about him that he was implementing the political will of the leadership.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the beginning of his answer due to the overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just please slow down. Start from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that Stanisic embarked immediately on --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you have to wait until my question is finished, sir.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. I think that in his second term of office, Stanisic fiercely launched a campaign of settling scores with the Speaker of the Assembly, Krajisnik, and all the other people around him. I primarily refer to the struggle that they had with relation to the commission of crimes. Let me finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm going to read out to you a portion of your statement, and I would just like to ask you whether you agree. And I'm doing that due to time constraints.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are starting to behave like the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I would very much like if I had more time to discuss with you, but, as you heard, the Trial Chamber has reminded me of my time limitation. Now, this is a transcript of the conversation you had. Unfortunately, I don't have the exact date, but it is marked T0002323 through 2331. That's page 17 of 232 in the Serbian, and it says: "So it means that Stanisic is in power only for seven or eight months and then he is dismissed. Zika Rakic is brought to fill his place and he entered into conflict later on, although he was a person in whom the party had enormous trust because the previous Minister Stanisic did not want to succumb to the political will during his second term of office. They didn't dare give me the position of the minister with all the powers. Instead they chose Zivko Rakic who was a trusted member of the SDS and whose duty was not to interfere too much in his own job." Is that more or less what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And, lastly, one more question. Sir, at the beginning, you and I discussed the situation in which towards the end of 1992 and the dismissal of Mico Stanisic and the bringing of Ratko Adzic as minister, everything had to start from scratch. And perhaps the situation was even worse than it had originally been, and you agreed with me. Tell me, in your opinion, and in view of the initial results and the objectives that you set out in 1992, had Mico Stanisic not been dismissed, would you have succeeded in persevering and establishing the MUP in a proper way and would all members of the MUP who committed crimes, as well as other perpetrators, have been brought before justice? I asked about your opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours. Objection. That calls --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before you answer the question. Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That calls for speculation, Your Honour. He has not been called to testify as an expert witness. This is pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic -- I have -- I agree, Mr. Hannis, that -- I -- I'd -- your -- your question would invite speculation upon speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness remained in MUP, and he explained at length what was the intention and what was the policy of the ministry in 1992. He also explained what was the situation in 1993. I'm just asking him, does he think that, in case they continued, that they would have achieved their goal? Was there that -- their intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- the "what ifs" of history, as of life, Mr. Zecevic, while fascinating, don't offer useful answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I understand, Your Honours. I don't have any further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Kovac. This is all I wanted to ask you. Have a nice day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see that it is almost time for a break, so shall I start or maybe we can make --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Perhaps we could take the break now, and have you any idea of how long you think you would be?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think 30, 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So we take the break and return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Cross examination by Mr. Krgovic:

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Kovac.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Dragan Krgovic, and on behalf of Zupljanin Defence team, I'm going to ask you a few questions relating to your evidence so far. I'm going to read a portion of the document that you discussed both with Mr. Zecevic and the Prosecutor. So could --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the witness please be shown 2D10-2038. It's tab --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Krgovic please repeat the tab number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, what you see before you is a personnel file of Simo Drljaca. Please go through the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, Your Honours, we have an English translation for some of the documents, but the whole file hasn't been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And I would kindly ask the witness just to leaf through the documents, and I would have two questions of general nature. Mr. Kovac, you will agree with me that in this personnel file of Mr. Drljaca there is no other document from 1992.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And if you look at page 2 of this document, this is what Mr. Zecevic was referring to, relating to Mr. Stakic's Defence team, to have proof of the appointment of Mr. Drljaca, and this is the response that they received, that this document did not exist in his file even back then; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what this documents says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, were you aware that in 1992, in order to have an unbroken service, some decisions were issued retroactively in order for certain individuals to cover specific periods, although they didn't have a proper legal decision?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that practice, although I never resorted to it. But I know that Ratko Adzic and Dragan Kijac did that. Unless somebody actually did some duties, I myself never issued such a decision when I was the minister. But there were was no need for that. People were not retiring at the time, and there was no need for such recourse.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kovac. Let us go back to a topic that you discussed with the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, lest I forget, can we have this entire document admitted into evidence but marked for identification because some parts of document haven't been translated yet. Provided there's no objection from Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection from me, Your Honour. It does duplicate some of the materials we already have. But, however, it does include one document, which is sort of a two-page form, which includes kind of his whole history in the MUP because it is counting the years of credit he has. That may be of some value. I don't know how Your Honours prefer to handle it. But I don't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The extended discussion which counsel would have observed that the Bench has had with the Registry -- with the Registry relates to what it is we're admitting. As I understand it, and the Registrar will correct me if I'm wrong, we already have, subject to Mr. Zecevic's satisfying himself with the accuracy of the numbering, the matter we dealt with this morning, we already have a portion of this as an exhibit. And the question is: What do we do those yet-to-be translated parts that Mr. Zecevic wishes to add. So it appears that once Mr. Zecevic has come on board, in terms of the -- what the existing exhibit is, the order that we would now make is that that exhibit be completed by the addition of -- of -- of the yet-to-be translated material. Clear as mud?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honours. I understand the concern about having duplicate exhibits, and I think it's impossible to avoid in a case of this size and complexity. I know in a recent review I did notice that we still have some cases where there is a P number for an exhibit, then the same document has a 1D number. But I have no objection to this whole thing coming in, and it makes sense it does. Now, whether you want to just admit this whole thing, and we'll use it for all things concerning the personnel documents of Mr. Drljaca. The trouble is we've had references to a different exhibit number a different document number with -- with the witness, but the ERN is the same, I think. So if we had this as the exhibit, I think maybe that would resolve the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The microphone might not have picked me up. The existing Exhibit P2462.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that has three or four separate documents out of this 28-page exhibit. This is the more complete document. I certainly have no objection to that being the one, and we can probably follow from the transcript because I think I mentioned specific ERN numbers or dates to the other ones when we identified them individually. If that makes sense, Your Honours, then we give this one a new number and it's basically the master document if we want to look at Simo Drljaca personnel documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's convenient to me, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So to summarise where we are, this is part of 2462, but the parties need to -- everybody has to have an understanding as to what makes up that -- that exhibit, and that's a detail that is still in process of being refined.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Maybe I can propose we make this 2462A, and we all understand that this is the master document, although I see that apparently is not a good idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm reminded that adding suffixes to exhibit numbers creates its own set of confusion, so, yeah...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, I'm going to show you a document, Exhibit P160. That's tab 1 of the Zupljanin Defence binder. For you to be able to follow what I'm asking more easily, I'll give you a hard copy. You won't find what I need in these binders in front of you, so you can put them away. It is document 1. See those yellow stickies on the side? Please go to page 5 in your copy. And, in e-court, it's page 8 of the Serbian, page 7 the English. While we're wait, let me ask you if you remember that the Prosecutor put it to you yesterday that the actions concerning these collection centres only began after the news broadcast on CNN, and you disagreed.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. I disagreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at the second paragraph from the top. We see what Mr. Zupljanin is saying at this meeting held on the 11th of July. It's about the army and Crisis Staffs and the conditions in the camps and the observance of norms. Please move on to document -- or, rather -- move to page 27. In Serbian, it's 30 -- in Serbian, in e-court, it's 30; and 25 is the English page number. These are the conclusions of the meeting. It's page 27 in your copy, sir. You see the conclusion of the senior officer. The fourth paragraph from the bottom, deal with the issue of collection centres, the jurisdiction of the relevant organs, and organising a joint meeting with the Ministry of Justice. Basically, Mr. Kovac, the solution of these problems, or, rather, the tackling of these problems begins then, and not as the Prosecutor put it to you, after the news on CNN; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment. I wasn't in charge of that, nor did I watch CNN. Our activities were continuous, and I pointed it out repeatedly, that what I did was not the final or -- that's a wrong choice of words. That was not an official application sent to the government. But, of course, as these problems were arising, we were dealing with them altogether. And I cannot speak about CNN because CNN means nothing to me. We followed these problems. We had documents that show the chronology of our actions in any part of the RS. And, of course, it's chronologically connected with the problems that existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, the Prosecutor showed you minutes yesterday, minutes of the extended collegium session of the ministry, and you began to answer but you were interrupted. So I would like to pick up from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document, tab 105 in the Prosecution binder. 65 ter 20218.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You will see it on the screen. You don't -- there's no hard copy for you. Page 4 in the Serbian and in the English also. These people were present, and you spoke about the commission from the Banja Luka CSB. You can see that the last person mentioned represents the commission for the administration of the CSB and SJB. I'm reading the last paragraph now. Branimir Pecanac, on behalf of the commission for the administration of the CSB and SJB. And what you said about managing the CSB Banja Luka at the time, it was managed by that commission, that group of people, then; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, you provided detailed answered to the Prosecutor about events from September 1993 until the establishment of this working group. At that time, Stojan Zupljanin didn't really manage the CSB, although, formally, he was at that position; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. He did a decision appointing him to that position, but the CSB was actually managed by the commission appointed by the government because, in Banja Luka, there was a state of emergency due to a military rebellion in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a mistake that I've just noticed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the state of emergency was proclaimed by the president and not the government; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the case, if I remember well. It must have been the president of the republic based on his authority. But I may be mistaken. I don't think it was the government though. But what it boils down to is that the CSB was managed by this commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, when you were examined by the Prosecutor and the Bench, you were painting a picture of the situation that prevailed in the MUP and the CSB at the time. You said that when the war began, the institutions of the internal affairs of Bosnia-Herzegovina fell apart, and that applies to Yugoslavia, too. And as from April, the MUP system did not operate probably?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if need be, I can clarify. Bosnia-Herzegovina, as different from the other republics -- there was simultaneously the dissolution of Yugoslavia and the dissolution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the state was dissolving institutionally and with regard to the system of values. What do I mean when I say "institutionally"? When there is a conflict in an area and the joint army, the JNA, is no longer operational, it doesn't exist, and there's interethnic conflict, that type of war where civilians -- where there were conflicting civilians, then the military dimension becomes impossible to control and you cannot speak of an organised state. There are negative processes if the society and the state are dissolving. And the institutions that were established, or at least officially envisaged, I mean, the MUP of the RS and the Crisis Staffs, they were embryo of the state and step by step they were being put under control and they, in turn, enable other institutions of the state to start operating, such as the public prosecutors' offices and the Ministry of Justice. So, in parallel, there is the function of the Army of the Republika Srpska which puts the armed people under the control of a military structure. So this is this transition. And the same was happening on the other side. There was an undefined mass where it is difficult to tell a fighter from a soldier, and on -- on the one hand and a civilian on the other hand. I'm, first of all, referring to men. So there were groups that were in conflict with each other. And it all depended on the power and the -- the swiftness of the leadership that -- to -- how and when they would be able to establish a sort of ground zero. And then the conditions were very similar to those in any civil war, be it in the Congo or anywhere else. The events were very similar. Only the difference is in the outcome, which powers eventually managed to gain control over the entire area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us look at document P621 now; tab 6 in the Zupljanin Defence binder. Mr. Kovac, you spoke rather extensively about the influence of the local authorities, the local Crisis Staffs, on the functioning of the MUP bodies. I now show you this report on the work of the Banja Luka CSB from 31 July till 30 September 1992. Now, please, go to page 20 in your hard copy; whereas, in e-court, it's 43 in Serbian and also in English. Here, Mr. Zupljanin, in his report, deals with some of the matters you have just spoken about. And in sentence one he says: "Generally speaking, it appears that the situation is increasingly getting out of control of the organs of legal authority, which is partly within the zone of responsibility of security organs and services." That was the beginning of paragraph 1. Now paragraph 2. He speaks more specifically about these things. I quote: "Inefficiency, lack of professionalism and superficiality of work in a number of SJBs contributed to a large extent to the functional detachment of a number of SJBs from the centre. This has gravely affected the overall unity and the social role of the security organs and services." Mr. Zupljanin goes on to say, I quote: "Parallel to that, some of the SJBs connected themselves with local politics and local political leaders, thereby neglecting their legal obligations and powers." In the last paragraph Mr. Zupljanin says the following --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. If the Defence is conceding that Mr. Zupljanin offered that report, I'll accept that, but his name doesn't appear on it, his signature doesn't appear on it, and I don't know if we've had any evidence to that effect. He can say this is the report from the CSB Banja Luka, but I don't know if it is was prepared by Mr. Zupljanin or the -- some other worker.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would just like to show the last page of this document -- actually, the last-but-one page in e-court, where we will see Mr. Zupljanin's signature. I believe that there can be no doubt about this being Mr. Zupljanin's signature, but if the Prosecutor still fosters some doubts. Oh, this is a Prosecution Exhibit, by the way, and so far it has not been disputed that Mr. Zupljanin is author of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll accept that, Your Honour. It doesn't appear referenced in the English translation I have in the binder I received from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us return to what we are talking about, Mr. Kovac. Do you agree with me, sir, that the situation was like this not only in the territory covered by the CSB Banja Luka but almost in the entire RS territory during that period from the start of the conflict almost until the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree. There were such problems in the whole territory, but we can see from this that the Banja Luka CSB professionally registered all events, and we see what their attitude toward them is, and I never denied that. However, if we are to analyse this document, you'll see that no mention is made of the MUP. I mean, MUP headquarters. And that's a problem that I've always pointed out. They needed the assistance of the entire MUP. I mean, a -- the MUP as a system, the MUP as a force. They were the largest centre, and they are clearly stating that they are unable to cope with the problems identified. So what was the way out? Only the strengthening of the Ministry of Interior. I won't say that there were differences between us there. But our assessment was with regard to Mr. Zupljanin that they were unable to cope with the problems in their area. That the ministry, as a whole, had to act and crack down on problems one by one. That has to do with the efficiency of the MUP, and it has also to do with political power. The chief of the centre obviously needed the political power of the minister of the interior and all of us in the ministry in order to resolve these problems. They are clearly outlining the problems and the problems really were the way they described them, and they had a good attitude, the correct attitude toward those problems, but I always kept repeating the power to solve these problems -- and this is not a criticism. We, as the higher-ranking body, knew about that. And we were physically able to reach them. I believe that after this point in time, the situation started improving, once we had linked up physically. And that is the need for processes applied by the ministry because we wanted to focus on one territorial body and help it to solve all their problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I fully agree with you, Mr. Kovac, and I think that was the view held by Mr. Zupljanin. I will show you a document where this is precisely what Mr. Zupljanin said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown P624.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Which is behind tab 7 in your binder. This is the report -- or, rather, yes, the report behind tab 7. It's a report on the work of the centre for an entire year. Let's look at the page where the programme was listed for the entire centre. It's the last page of the document. It reads here -- and please look at the last paragraph, more extensive co-operation with the MUP on co-ordinating tasks of internal affairs. Of course, the problem up to that point was since there was no physical contact, no assistance could have been given; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was an issue for us, the fact that we were not physically connected. We had to work on that and we had to raise awareness on their part that without a proper MUP, we would not be able to address the problem properly and within the ambit of the law, especially in view of the political difficulties they were in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, when it comes to the problems that we believe existed objectively in Republika Srpska, the problem that was peculiar for the Banja Luka CSB was the fact that out of some 15 public security stations that existed there before the war, it mushroomed into an organisation of 26 public security stations that existed in 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. At some point, and for a brief period of time, a political concept was being entertained of the SAO Krajina with its government and its various agencies. I was explaining that the SAOs constituted a psychological and operational problem for us on our way to put together the MUP as an executive branch. And one of the problems that Stanisic had with Koroman at Pale was the functioning of the SAO Romanija and the related stations. This was a general occurrence and a process. At some point, the SAOs had a role of getting organised and moving to become independent from the central organs in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And since that had gone further down the road, it was very difficult for us to reintegrate them into a single state security system, complete with all the other difficulties that we had including civil war, war, destruction in general, and other processes that were disruptive of the social tissue for the people, as such, as well as the institutions at large.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As a result of that process, the Banja Luka CSB was far too large to be able to function efficiently. It had to be divided up into a number of smaller centres which was, in fact, done at last in late 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we -- we annexed some of these parts to the Doboj CSB and proceeded to put together a CSB in Prijedor. In other words, we would have three centres. Not only that, we organised other republican institutions in the area, such as, for instance, the elements of the special police brigade, elements of crime services and forensic examination, institutions. Plus, we had our own detached MUP offices in these areas. All these were necessary measures in order for us to set things on the right course and provide meaningful assistance to making these services efficient. And, of course, let me add that there was a -- an open division between state and public security bodies so that the CSB chief no longer had within his remit the state security structure. In other words, the CSB chief had a reduced scope of duties by that token.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And, in fact, only after you had applied these measures were the conditions put in place for the Banja Luka CSB to operate properly in keeping with the law and the regulations governing the work of the organs of internal affairs?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after the September events which made it apparent to the political and military leadership of the Krajina what it meant to obstruct the work of state organs, only after those events were we able to make it clear to them that there should not be improper political influence and that there should be proper relations between the various state administration bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kovac. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, we thank you for your coming to assist the Tribunal by your testimony. You are now released, and we wish you a safe journey back to your home. We are not going to rise immediately. We have certain administrative matters with which to deal, so I would invite the usher to escort you from the courtroom. And, Mr. Lazarevic, we thank you for your assistance, and you are free to withdraw, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, first of all, have you been able to satisfy yourself as to the accuracy of the numbers of those -- the exhibits that -- that we have?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I do have -- I do have all -- all the -- all the actual pages if -- it refers to four documents concerning -- from the file of Mr. Drljaca, four pages, and three pages from the file of Mr. Koroman. And I believe everything has been in order. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Right, so exhibit [Microphone not activated]. Exhibits 2461 and P2462 are now in order. Am I correct, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Oh yes, sorry. Subject to the addition of the -- of the yet-to-be translated documents. Any there any other matters that counsel wish to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had been requested to at some point in time put on the record some changes that made to exhibits in e-court, but I don't know that we need necessarily do that today because I anticipate at some time in the near future we probably need to have some sort of administrative hearing to deal with some unresolved matters and setting of the date for the final trial brief and closing submissions, et cetera. I note we had general parameters, but I think we still have to resolve the matter of Mr. Zecevic's submission and the final decision on the consolidated hyperlinked spreadsheet, the POD, and I think there was a Prosecution's request to perhaps call two witnesses. And so until those matters are finally resolved, I think we can't have a firm date for the final trial brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What the Chamber wishes to say is that with the conclusion of the testimony of its own witnesses, it will issue its decisions on the outstanding motions which relate to evidence in due course, and the dates for the final briefs an arguments will be tied to the date that the last decision on evidence is issued, and these dates will be specified for the parties in the forthcoming Scheduling Order. So I trust the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, the advice to me that inasmuch as notwithstanding what I have just said, there is a possibility that we may not have to formally sit again. Whether you are -- I'm to inquire as to whether you are able now to deal with these -- sorting out these 65 ter numbers or whether you would be -- you would prefer to deal with it subsequently -- [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I can do it now, Your Honour. I have a list of some 15 or 20 documents to which changes have been made in e-court, such as translations uploaded, et cetera. That's what I have. But it sounds like perhaps you're talking about something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The view seems to be that there would be no harm in your doing it subsequently in writing. But you -- what you have before you is the -- is the matters in which we were inquiring.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But I think it's been a tough week and it's Friday and this is not the most exciting stuff, and I think it could be adequately handled with a written, or I could just attach this. For example, item 1 is: Exhibit P00034, unofficial transcript of testimony has been replaced with official transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It seems to me it would be more efficient and more practical to do it in writing, because we're dealing with numbers and it's quite easy in terms of the transcript for --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That would please me, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, you seem to be rising.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I have a submission to make. In the past couple of weeks we received huge material from the Prosecution under Rule 68. These were interviews and testimonies of certain witnesses that we have been disclosed with only now. Based on the information I received from my learned friends from the OTP, the disclosure process has not been completed yet and we are soon to receive more such material. Your Honours, the material is, and Ms. Korner agrees with me on this score, clearly exculpatory for a my client. The Defence needs to go through the material, and I wanted to let Their Honours know that perhaps - we are still considering the possibility - we will file a motion in some ten days do re-open the Defence case for Mr. Zupljanin in order to have some of these statements and testimonies admitted into evidence. I am telling you this by way of an announcement so that it wouldn't come as a surprise. We are still in the process of going through the material that we received only recently. I know the difficulties the Prosecution have with the searches of the material that they have. The material has surfaced at some point to their surprise. Therefore, I wanted to put Their Honours on notice of our probable filing within -- in due time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, one other point just before you go. I understand that there will be some Scheduling Order forthcoming. I wonder if you are able to indicate to us today before you leave if there's a not-before-date by which the final trial brief will not be due in terms of it will not be due before Easter, or it will not be due before Queen's Day at the end of April. Just to give us general parameters, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, even I were inclined to agree with that as a purely sensible suggestion, the alert that Mr. Krgovic has just indicated, that, of course, is in the context of the ongoing disclosure obligation which the Prosecution has, it may be imprudent for the Chamber to say that at this point. So we take things, as usual, one step at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it seems that the gist of what Mr. Krgovic has indicated will not do anything to make the date earlier than it already is. It would only make it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, to the extent that some small measure of comfort may be afforded you, as of today we could say it would not be before Easter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So, with that, we take the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
